pages.text: Bespoke Luxury Journeys Feel the world differently. We design highly exclusive, privately guided expeditions through Vietnam. No templates, no schedules—simply the art of travel, recomposed for you. Design Your Journey Explore Expeditions Signature Cruise Traditional Luxury Junks in Ha Long Bay Spend a quiet night sailing past limestone towers on a private, single-cabin wooden junk. Our Philosophy We curate extraordinary travel moments The finest journeys are not merely planned—they are composed. Shaped around your unique cadence, our signature expeditions connect you with the deep soul of Vietnam. From misty northern terraces to the silent, winding waters of the Mekong, we curate travel that feels entirely, fortuitously yours. Begin Your Tale Travel Inspiration Where are you waiting to discover? North Inspiration Central Heritage Southern & Food Trekking in Sapa A first-hand guide to Sapa's mountain kingdom, ethnic minority villages, and golden terraced rice fields. Read Trekking Guide Halong Bay vs Lan Ha Bay An honest comparison between the iconic Halong Bay and the pristine Lan Ha Bay to help you choose the best voyage. Read Cruise Guide VIEW ALL TRAVEL GUIDES The Bespoke Process Expeditions that feel like they were waiting You are not meant to see Vietnam like everyone else. You are meant to feel it, like only you can. It is why our designers use their deep local insight to craft moments that feel fortuitously right. 01 Uncovering your motivations We spend time learning what truly drives your curiosity. Rather than suggesting cookie-cutter routes, we start with a blank page. 02 Handcrafting your unique route Every hotel, private transfer, and local dining recommendation is handpicked by a designer who has personally vetted them. 03 Hosting you at every single step Our local concierge is active 24/7 on the ground. From VIP airport tracks to sudden itinerary changes, you are fully hosted. A single ribbon of silk, drawn the length of the coast. Our signature fourteen-night passage — north to south, mountain to delta. Every stop below can be lengthened, shortened, or set aside entirely. 01 Hanoi Days 1–2 · Old Quarter & French Quarter 02 Halong Bay Days 3–5 · Private Junk 03 Hue Days 6–7 · Imperial Citadel 04 Hoi An Days 8–10 · Ancient Town 05 Saigon Days 11–12 · District 1 06 Mekong Delta Days 13–14 · River Passage 01 Hanoi Days 1–2 · Old Quarter & French Quarter 02 Halong Bay Days 3–5 · Private Junk 03 Hue Days 6–7 · Imperial Citadel 04 Hoi An Days 8–10 · Ancient Town 05 Saigon Days 11–12 · District 1 06 Mekong Delta Days 13–14 · River Passage Inspirations Possibilities, not packages Only you decide where your journey will take you. These custom curated itineraries are just possibilities to inspire you for an expedition that is as individual as you. The emerald terraces, the warm smiles of our local Hmong hosts.” “Wandering the lantern-lit canals of Hoi An after midnight, we felt as though we had stepped back into another century.” “Our specialist managed to arrange a private meeting with a calligraphy master in Hanoi—an unforgettable window into Vietnamese art.” “Floating down the peaceful backwaters of the Mekong, watching the river life drift by, was the ultimate peace we were seeking.” Design Desk Compose Your Private Expedition Connect with a Design Specialist +84 988600388 BEGIN YOUR EXPEDITION Inspirations Request our Vietnam lookbook Our private edition Vietnam lookbook contains curated tailor-made itineraries, boutique cruise vessel profiles, and heritage destination guides to help you start planning your bespoke Vietnam holiday from the UK. REQUEST A LOOKBOOK Our Distinction Why journey with us? Bespoke Pacing No group plans. We handcraft the entire journey around your personal speed and interests. Handpicked Storytellers Private local scholars, historians, and guides who bring Vietnam's rich heritage to life. Signature Retreats Access to private boutique traditional cruises, historic hotels, and sustainable luxury ecolodges. Seamless Logistics From VIP airport fast-track arrival services to private transfers, we handle every detail 24/7.

pages.text: Luxury Resorts & Hotels Home > Hotels 50 Vietnam Tours 14 Travel Guides 11 Places to visit 6 Hotels 6 Things to do 0 Vietnam Cruises 12 Best time to visit Elite Hideaways Luxury Resorts & Lodges We have handpicked only the finest properties in Vietnam. From remote clifftop pool villas overlooking Vinh Hy Bay to heritage palaces in Hanoi, these stays guarantee premium luxury. 5-Star Ultra-Luxury Amanoi Vinh Hy Bay, Ninh Thuan Province Claiming a spectacular stretch of Vietnam’s mountainous coastline within Nui Chua National Park, Amanoi is a natural sanctuary overlooking Vinh Hy Bay. Meaning "place of peace," the resort fits seamlessly into the pristine landscape, offering private pavilions, multi-bedroom villas, and an exceptional wellness spa. Private Plunge Pool Personal Butler Service Hilltop Infinity Pool Explore Resort → Official Site ↗ 5-Star Luxury Eco-Resort Six Senses Ninh Van Bay Ninh Van Bay, Nha Trang Six Senses Ninh Van Bay sits on a dramatic bay that gives the feeling of being on an island. Impressive rock formations, a white sand beach, and towering mountains behind add to the fantasy. The resort offers spacious pool villas nestled on the beach, perched over water, or hidden in the tropical jungle. Overwater & Hilltop Villas Wine Cave Dining Pristine Coral Reef Access Explore Resort → Official Site ↗ 5-Star Historic Palace Sofitel Legend Metropole Hanoi Hoan Kiem, Hanoi A prominent landmark in the heart of Hanoi since 1901, the Sofitel Legend Metropole Hanoi has a long-standing history of hosting royalty, heads of state, and legendary writers. Blending French colonial grandeur with neo-classical elegance, this award-winning heritage hotel features luxurious rooms, Michelin-recommended dining, and a hidden wartime bunker. Historic French-Colonial Wing Michelin-selected Restaurant Bespoke Sommelier Service Explore Resort → Official Site ↗ 5-Star Modern Ultra-Luxury Regent Phu Quoc Long Beach, Phu Quoc Island An ultra-luxury beachfront sanctuary located on Phu Quoc’s tranquil Long Beach, Regent Phu Quoc offers a stunning mix of modern design and Vietnamese hospitality. The resort is designed to be a personal haven, featuring massive suites and pool villas, private lagoons, and unparalleled dining experiences curated by global chefs. Private Lagoon Villas Ocean View Sky Pools Omakase & Fine Dining Explore Resort → Official Site ↗ 5-Star Ultra-Luxury Four Seasons Resort The Nam Hai Ha My Beach, Hoi An A luxurious beachfront oasis along the pristine Ha My Beach, Four Seasons Resort The Nam Hai offers a seamless portal to three UNESCO World Heritage sites. The resort features elegant pool villas, tranquil infinity pools, and a world-class spa floating on a lotus-filled lagoon. Private Beachfront Villas Three Tiered Infinity Pools Heart of the Earth Spa Explore Resort → Official Site ↗ 5-Star Boutique Luxury Capella Hanoi Hoan Kiem, Hanoi Located just steps from the iconic Hanoi Opera House, Capella Hanoi is a boutique masterpiece designed by Bill Bensley. Celebrating the glamorous opera era of the 1920s, the hotel features individual suites themed after opera legends, a Michelin-starred restaurant, and an opulent indoor pool. Bill Bensley Art-Deco Suites Michelin-Starred Hibana Restaurant Auriga Spa & Royal Pool Explore Resort → Official Site ↗

Travel Tips 4 Jul 2026 Best Places to Visit in Vietnam: A Local Operator's Complete Guide (2026) Our Ho Chi Minh City–based guides have visited every destination on this list within the past 12 months. Here is what we actually found — including the things the tourist brochures never tell you.
18 Jun 2026 The Ultimate 14-Day Vietnam Itinerary: A British Guide to Going Private The Ultimate 2-Week Vietnam Itinerary: A British Guide to Doing It Right

1 Jun 2025 Vietnam by Fork: The Ultimate Culinary Tour from Hanoi to Saigon Vietnamese cuisine is not one cuisine — it is three. Hanoi's food is austere and precise. Central Vietnam's is fiery and ceremonial. Saigon's is abundant and influenced by the south's sugar cane and coconut milk. A culinary tour connecting all three is one of the most rewarding ways to travel this extraordinary country.

20 May 2025 Hoi An: The Complete Guide to Vietnam's Most Beautiful Town Hoi An's Ancient Town is a UNESCO gem of perfectly preserved merchant architecture, lantern-lit streets, and extraordinary food. But the secret Hoi An — the bicycle rides through the rice paddies, the fishing villages, the uncrowded beach — is just as rewarding and far less photographed.

8 May 2025 Hanoi: The Essential City Guide for Discerning Travellers Vietnam's capital is often dismissed as a transit stop to Halong Bay. It is a serious mistake. Hanoi rewards slow exploration: its French colonial architecture, lake-side temples, extraordinary food scene, and quietly ferocious art culture deserve at least three days of genuine attention.

22 Apr 2025 The Mekong Delta: How to Do It Properly (Without a Group Tour) The Mekong Delta is the rice bowl of Vietnam — a vast, flat, river-threaded landscape where life has moved by sampan for centuries. Most visitors do it on a day tour from Saigon and see almost nothing. Here is how to do it in two days, properly, with a private boat and a guide who actually lives here.

15 Apr 2025 What Does a Truly Luxury Vietnam Tour Actually Look Like? After a decade of designing luxury itineraries in Vietnam, I have a clear answer to the question I am asked most often: what separates a luxury Vietnam tour from an expensive one? The difference is almost entirely in the details — and the details are everything.

5 Apr 2025 First Time in Vietnam: Everything You Need to Know Before You Go Vietnam rewards those who arrive prepared. After years of taking travellers here for the first time, I have distilled the essential knowledge into one guide — visas, money, health, etiquette, and the one mistake every first-timer makes.

28 Mar 2025 Ha Giang: Vietnam's Most Spectacular Landscape (and How to Reach It) Ha Giang Province, in Vietnam's far north, is 300 kilometres of limestone peaks, river gorges, and Hmong villages that most tourists never see. The road here is extraordinary. The food is memorable. The silence is absolute.

12 Mar 2025 2 Weeks in Vietnam: The Definitive Private Tour Itinerary (2025) I spent two unforgettable weeks travelling Vietnam from Hanoi to Ho Chi Minh City with a private guide. Here is every destination, every hotel, and the exact route that worked brilliantly — so you can replicate it or tweak it to your tastes.

18 Feb 2025 Halong Bay vs Lan Ha Bay: Which Should You Choose (and Why Not Both)? I have slept on a junk in both Halong Bay and Lan Ha Bay. They are 20 kilometres apart and worlds different in character. Here is the honest comparison — including the version that gives you the best of both in a single voyage.

5 Feb 2025 Phu Quoc Island: Vietnam's Most Refined Beach Destination Phu Quoc has transformed from a forgotten fishing island into Vietnam's leading beach destination in a decade. Done correctly — with a villa property rather than a resort block, private beach access, and time for the island's still-excellent fish sauce trail — it is genuinely extraordinary.

30 Jan 2025 Trekking in Sapa: A First-Hand Guide to Vietnam's Mountain Kingdom At 1,600 metres above sea level, Sapa's terraced rice paddies and ethnic minority villages create one of the most visually extraordinary landscapes in Asia. I trekked here in October — the best month — and discovered a region that rewards those who choose a private guide over a group tour.

jsonLd.description: Our Ho Chi Minh City–based guides have visited every destination on this list within the past 12 months. Here is what we actually found — including the things the tourist brochures never tell you.

pages.text: Travel Tips # vietnam # destinations Best Places to Visit in Vietnam: A Local Operator's Complete Guide (2026) Tuấn Nguyễn Senior Vietnam Travel Specialist · Vietnam Tours, since 2012 Published 4 Jul 2026 Reading Time 6 MIN READ 50 Vietnam Tours 14 Travel Guides 11 Places to visit 6 Hotels 6 Things to do 0 Vietnam Cruises 12 Best time to visit Information last verified and updated: October 2026 Disclosure: This article may contain affiliate links to hotels, tours, or booking platforms. If you book through our links, we may earn a small commission at no extra cost to you. All opinions are based on our team's real, first-hand experiences in Vietnam. “ Our Ho Chi Minh City–based guides have visited every destination on this list within the past 12 months. Here is what we actually found — including the things the tourist brochures never tell you. ” Vietnam is one of those countries that genuinely rewards slow travel. The country stretches more than 1,600km from north to south, and each region has a completely different character — different climate, different food, different pace. After running private tours here since 2012, our team has developed strong opinions about where to go, how long to spend, and — just as importantly — what the usual advice gets wrong. This guide is based on visits our own guides made in 2025 and 2026. Where we have noticed a problem at a destination — poor infrastructure, overcrowding, tourist-targeted pricing — we say so directly. Our goal is to help you make a genuinely informed decision, not to sell you on everywhere. Hanoi Hanoi is a city that requires time to appreciate. First impressions are often chaotic — the traffic on the ring roads is punishing, the heat in summer is intense, and the Old Quarter feels crowded with souvenir shops. Give it two full days and it changes entirely. The 36 guild streets each have a different personality, the temple courtyards are quieter than they look from the street, and the lakeside café culture is genuinely lovely. Insider: The best cà phê trứng (egg coffee) in the city is not at Cafe Giang on Nguyen Huu Huan — that one is famous and always rammed with tourists. Walk five minutes to Dinh Tien Hoang Street and try the version at the small shopfront with no English sign, run by a woman in her 60s. It costs 25,000 VND, the custard is thicker, and you will have the entire upstairs terrace to yourself most mornings. Honest assessment: The night market on Hang Dao is almost entirely the same mass-produced goods you'll find in every city in Southeast Asia. Skip it unless you enjoy that kind of browsing. The Temple of Literature is genuinely worth the 70,000 VND entrance fee and a quiet hour on a weekday morning — avoid Sunday afternoons when it fills with local graduation photo sessions. See our Hanoi destination guide and Hanoi day tours for detailed itineraries. Ha Long Bay The limestone formations really do look exactly like the photographs — at dawn, with low mist sitting between the towers, it is one of the most dramatic landscapes in Southeast Asia. Our guide Linh visited in March 2026 and described it as 'still extraordinary, but you have to choose your boat carefully.' Insider: The busiest routes run through the central zone, roughly around Ti Top Island and Sung Sot Cave. Request a boat that focuses on the southern Lan Ha Bay area instead — same geology, dramatically fewer tour boats, and access to some beaches that are genuinely empty by 7am. The difference in atmosphere between the two zones is significant. Honest assessment: Some of the cheaper overnight cruises (under £80 per person) have poorly maintained bathrooms, thin mattresses, and group meal tables that seat 20 strangers. The activity schedule is often rushed. Spend a little more for a boat with fewer than 16 cabins. The itinerary will be almost identical but the experience is night-and-day different. Compare cruise options in our Ha Long Bay destination guide or browse luxury Ha Long Bay cruise packages . Hoi An Hoi An is the most reliably beautiful town in Vietnam. The ancient quarter — genuinely preserved wooden merchant houses, narrow lanes, Japanese bridge — is walkable, human-scaled, and lit beautifully by lanterns every evening. Our guide Tuấn visited in June 2026 and still calls it his favourite place in the country after 14 years of working here. Insider: The tailors along Tran Phu Street accept same-day orders and produce reasonable work. But the tailors who do outstanding work are usually found off the main road — ask your hotel reception who they personally recommend, not who pays them a referral fee. Budget a minimum of three fittings over two days if you want something genuinely well-made. The biggest mistake guests make is ordering 4 items in 24 hours and expecting perfection. Honest assessment: Hoi An is genuinely crowded in peak season (December–February). The ancient town zone fills with tour groups between 9am and 4pm. If you are staying overnight — which we strongly recommend — the old town empties significantly after 9pm and the atmosphere becomes magical. An Bang beach, 4km away, is the local favourite and far less busy than Cua Dai. See our full Hoi An destination guide including the Hoi An Farming & Fishing day tour and cooking class in Hoi An . Phong Nha-Ke Bang National Park Phong Nha is the most underrated destination in Vietnam. The cave system here is the largest on earth — Paradise Cave alone is 31km long and has cathedral-sized chambers with formations that look genuinely surreal. Our guide Linh visited in April 2026 and described the experience as 'the most viscerally impressive thing I have done in 10 years of guiding.' Insider: Paradise Cave is significantly better than Phong Nha Cave for the main cave experience, despite being less famous. Phong Nha Cave (the boat cave) is shorter and more commercialised, but the boat ride on the underground river is genuinely beautiful. Book both for a full day and hire a private guide rather than joining a group — the difference in information quality is substantial. Entry to Paradise Cave is 250,000 VND per person (verified April 2026). Honest assessment: The Dark Cave (zipline + mudbath) is fun but very commercial. The zip line itself is about 400m over a lake and takes approximately 30 seconds — manage expectations accordingly. Son Doong, the world's largest cave, requires a multi-day permit-only expedition costing approximately £2,500 per person and books out years in advance. See our Phong Nha destination guide with verified entry prices and recommended cave routes. Ho Chi Minh City (Saigon) Ho Chi Minh City is where our team is based, so we visit it constantly. It is the most immediately energetic city in Vietnam — faster, louder, and more commercially driven than Hanoi. District 1 contains most of the major historical sites within easy walking distance of each other: the War Remnants Museum, the Reunification Palace, Notre-Dame Cathedral (currently under scaffolding for restoration as of 2026), the General Post Office. Insider: The War Remnants Museum is genuinely harrowing and requires at least two hours. Go early (it opens at 7:30am) to avoid school groups. The ground floor US military equipment exhibition is the least emotionally demanding place to start. The third floor photographic exhibitions are devastating and deeply important. Do not underestimate how much emotional energy it takes — build a quiet afternoon into your schedule afterwards. We run a popular Saigon street food vespa evening tour and a Cu Chi Tunnels half-day excursion — both consistently rated our most-requested HCMC experiences. When to Visit Vietnam Vietnam's climate divides roughly into three zones. The north (Hanoi, Sapa, Ha Long) is best October–April, with a genuine winter in December–January that can require a light jacket. The central coast (Hue, Da Nang, Hoi An) runs best February–August — the rainy season peaks in October and November, when flooding in Hoi An's ancient town is a real issue. The south (Saigon, Mekong, Phu Quoc) is best November–April, the dry season. Our Best Time to Visit Vietnam guide breaks down monthly weather patterns for each region with real temperature and rainfall data. Planning Your Vietnam Trip Browse our Vietnam itineraries for sample routes, or read our Vietnam visa guide for up-to-date e-visa requirements. If you would prefer to speak with someone directly, contact our team — we are based in Vietnam and answer within one working day. Written by Tuấn Nguyễn Senior Vietnam Travel Specialist · Vietnam Tours, since 2012 Tuấn has guided over 400 private tours across Vietnam since 2012. He was born in Hanoi, grew up in Hoi An, and now lives in Ho Chi Minh City — which means he knows the quirks of every region firsthand. His specialty is designing honest, unhurried itineraries for repeat travellers who want to go beyond the surface. pages.text: The Ultimate 14-Day Vietnam Itinerary: A British Guide to Going Private Published 18 Jun 2026 Reading Time 5 MIN READ 50 Vietnam Tours 14 Travel Guides 11 Places to visit 6 Hotels 6 Things to do 0 Vietnam Cruises 12 Best time to visit Information last verified and updated: October 2026 Disclosure: This article may contain affiliate links to hotels, tours, or booking platforms. If you book through our links, we may earn a small commission at no extra cost to you. All opinions are based on our team's real, first-hand experiences in Vietnam. “ The Ultimate 2-Week Vietnam Itinerary: A British Guide to Doing It Right ” For most of us in the UK, booking a trip to Southeast Asia is the ultimate annual leave reward. And if Vietnam is on your radar, you’re in for an absolute treat. It’s got everything: the beautiful chaos of Hanoi, the surreal limestone karsts of Halong Bay, and that distinct, slow-paced charm of Hoi An. But here’s the catch: Vietnam is massive. It stretches over a thousand miles from north to south, and trying to squeeze it into a fortnight can easily turn your dream holiday into a stressful logistical military exercise. If you want to actually experience the country rather than just ticking boxes from a crowded tour bus window, here is how to spend a perfect 14 days in Vietnam - comfortably, deeply, and at your own pace. The Secret to Not Burning Out: Go Private Before talking about the route, let’s clear one thing up. Packing into a 45-seat coach with forty strangers might save a few quid, but it strips away the magic. On the flip side, navigating local trains and taxis on your own can be exhausting when time is short. This is why Vietnam private tours are the sweet spot for British travellers. Having your own air-conditioned car, a flexible schedule, and a local guide who knows where to find the best Phở (and when to avoid the tour buses) changes the entire game. You get the freedom of independent travel, but with none of the stress. Days 1–3: Diving into the Chaos of Hanoi Most flights from London Heathrow land straight into Hanoi. Give yourself that first afternoon just to unpack, combat the jet lag (it’s GMT+6 over here), and get your bearings. Hanoi is beautifully intense. Spend your days wandering through the labyrinth of the 36 streets in the Old Quarter, dodging scooters with practiced confidence, and sitting on tiny plastic stools by Ho Kiem Lake with a rich egg coffee. The Private Advantage: Instead of getting lost in the history, spend a morning with a private guide at the Temple of Literature and the Ho Chi Minh Mausoleum. They’ll give you the real, unvarnished stories behind the city’s complex French colonial and ancient past that you won’t find in a guidebook. Days 4–5: Waking Up on Halong Bay From Hanoi, it’s a smooth 2.5-hour drive down to the coast. You’ve likely seen a thousand photos of Halong Bay, but nothing quite prepares you for seeing those emerald-green waters and limestone giants in person. The trick here is to skip the cheap day-boats. Opt for an overnight cruise on a luxury boutique vessel. Even better, look for itineraries that head into Lan Ha Bay—it’s the quieter, less crowded neighbor to Halong, meaning you actually get to hear the water rather than other boat engines. You’ll spend the days kayaking into hidden sea caves and the evenings watching the sunset from the deck with a cold drink. Days 6–9: The Tailors and Heritage of Central Vietnam Next, a quick domestic flight brings you to the historic heart of the country: Hue and Hoi An. If you love history, you’ll want to spend a day exploring the sprawling Imperial Citadel in Hue and cruising down the Perfume River. Afterwards, take the scenic route over the famous Hai Van Pass to reach Hoi An. This lantern-lit ancient town is consistently a favourite for UK visitors. It’s entirely pedestrian-friendly, incredibly laid-back, and famous for its world-class tailoring. Insider Tip: If you want a custom linen suit or a bespoke dress, head straight to a reputable tailor on your first afternoon. They can whip up high-quality garments in 48 hours, leaving you plenty of time for final fittings while you spend your days cycling through local organic farms or relaxing by the river. Days 10–12: The Electric Energy of Saigon (Ho Chi Minh City) From the quiet charm of Hoi An, you’ll fly south into Vietnam’s commercial engine room. Ho Chi Minh City (still fondly called Saigon by locals) is a buzzing, modern metropolis where sleek skyscrapers sit right alongside French colonial landmarks. While you're here, a trip to the Cu Chi Tunnels is non-negotiable. It’s a sobering, fascinating look at the underground network used during the war. How to do it right: Have your private driver pick you up early in the morning. Arriving before the massive tour coaches arrive gives you a quiet, respectful environment to actually absorb the history. Days 13–14: Cruising the Mekong Delta & Heading Home Before catching your flight back to the UK, spend your final days exploring the "rice bowl" of Vietnam. The Mekong Delta is a world lived on the water. Swap your car for a private boutique sampan boat and drift through palm-lined canals. You'll see vibrant floating markets, watch local families making coconut candy, and get a glimpse of a timeless, rural way of life that feels a million miles away from Saigon's skyscrapers. On Day 14, your driver will take you back to Saigon’s airport for your overnight flight home. A Few Practical Bits for Brits Visas: Great news here—UK passport holders currently enjoy visa-free entry to Vietnam for stays up to 45 days. Just make sure your passport has at least 6 months of validity left. When to Go: To get the best weather across the whole country (since the north and south have completely different climates), aim for November to April. Money: The Vietnamese Dong (VND) makes everyone a millionaire instantly. While cards are fine in big hotels, you’ll want cash for the street food stalls and markets in Hoi An. Let’s Plan Your Journey At vietnamTours.co.uk, we don’t do cookie-cutter holiday packages. We design seamless, luxury private journeys tailored entirely around how you like to travel. We’ll handle the internal flights, the hand-picked boutique hotels, and the best local guides, so you can just focus on the adventure. pages.text: Region Overview Nestled in the Hoang Lien Son mountains of northwest Vietnam, Sapa is a premier trekking destination famous for its cascading golden rice terraces, misty mountain peaks, and rich cultural diversity. It overlooks the Muong Hoa Valley and stands in the shadow of Fansipan, Indochina's highest peak. The region is home to several ethnic minority groups, including the Black H'mong and Red Dzao. Traveling with a private local guide is highly recommended, as it supports the community and provides deep cultural insights into local weaving, agricultural traditions, and folklore. Top Highland Activities • Guided Valley Trekking: Walk along narrow dirt tracks through cascading green and golden rice terraces, passing through tribal villages like Cat Cat, Lao Chai, and Ta Van. • Indigenous Homestays: Spend a night in a traditional stilt house with an ethnic minority family, enjoying home-cooked meals and learning about their daily way of life. • Fansipan Peak: Ascend Indochina's highest peak (3,143m) via a scenic three-cable gondola ride, which glides above the cloud-veiled valleys and rugged pine forests. Key Region Highlights ✓ Trek through bamboo forests and terraced paddies ✓ Stay overnight in a H'Mong family homestay ✓ Explore vibrant weekend ethnic markets Tailormade Travel Planning Want to combine Sapa with other regions? pages.text: Best Time to Visit Vietnam Home > Best Time to Visit 50 Vietnam Tours 14 Travel Guides 11 Places to visit 6 Hotels 6 Things to do 0 Vietnam Cruises 12 Best time to visit The best time to visit Vietnam is between November and April . This is when the country experiences the least amount of rain and temperatures are highly comfortable. Northern Vietnam Hanoi, Halong Bay, Sapa, Ha Giang There are two distinct seasons. It's hot and humid from May to October with high rainfall, but the weather cools down from November to April and it's much drier. December and January can be quite cold in the highlands, with temperatures dropping below 10°C (50°F) in Sapa. Recommended Months: October – April Central Vietnam Hoi An, Hue, Da Nang, Nha Trang Central Vietnam's summer season lasts from January until the end of August. The weather is hot and dry, with temperatures ranging between 26°C and 35°C. Conditions between September and December are much wetter, with high rainfall and occasional tropical storms. Recommended Months: February – May Southern Vietnam Ho Chi Minh City, Mekong Delta, Phu Quoc Southern Vietnam's hot and dry season starts in November and finishes at the end of April, with temperatures often reaching 32°C - 35°C. Rain falls regularly between May and October, but the weather still remains warm, usually between 28°C and 32°C, with rainfall typically limited to brief afternoon downpours. JAN FEB MAR APR MAY JUN JUL AUG SEP OCT NOV DEC Monthly Breakdown Visiting Vietnam in January January is peak travel season in Vietnam, and for good reason. The country experiences some of its most pleasant weather of the year, though conditions vary dramatically from the chilly northern peaks to the sun-drenched beaches of the far south. If you are planning a comprehensive north-to-south journey, January offers a beautiful contrast of winter charm in Hanoi and tropical warmth in Phu Quoc. It is also the month leading up to Tet (Lunar New Year), meaning streets are filled with festive flower markets and dynamic preparations. Vietnam's geography creates three distinct climate zones. In the North (Hanoi, Halong Bay, Sapa), January is mid-winter. Temperatures average 15°C to 20°C (59°F to 68°F), with Sapa dropping below 10°C. You will experience cool, dry days often accompanied by atmospheric mist or light drizzle — ideal for city walking tours but requiring warm layers for the highlands. mainEntity.name: Is everything closed during Tet in February?

acceptedAnswer.text: During the official 3-4 days of Tet, many independent shops, markets, and restaurants close. However, major hotels, tourist sights, and some international restaurants remain open. Our tour guides continue to work, and we adjust itineraries to ensure a seamless experience.

mainEntity.name: Is February a busy month for tourism in Vietnam?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, February is peak season. Both international tourists and domestic families travel heavily, especially around Tet. We recommend booking flights, hotels, and cruises at least 4-6 months in advance.

pages.text: IDEAS BY MONTH Vietnam in February: Weather, Places to Go & Festivals Home > Ideas by Month > February 50 Vietnam Tours 14 Travel Guides 11 Places to visit 6 Hotels 6 Things to do 0 Vietnam Cruises 12 Best time to visit February is one of the most popular months to visit Vietnam. The cold winter of the north begins to lift, central Vietnam enjoys warm and dry weather, and the south remains hot and sunny. It is also the month most frequently associated with Tet, the Vietnamese Lunar New Year, offering travellers a rare window into the nation's most sacred cultural celebrations. The Spring Climate and Regional Guide In Northern Vietnam, February brings a transition from winter to spring. Temperatures rise to a comfortable 17°C to 22°C, though misty mornings and light drizzle are still common. Sapa begins to warm up, and wild peach and plum trees burst into white and pink blossoms across the highlands. Central Vietnam experiences excellent weather in February. The rains are gone, and temperatures rise to 22°C - 26°C. Cities like Hue and Hoi An are at their most beautiful, with mild humidity and ample sunshine. Southern Vietnam continues its run of perfect dry-season weather. Temperatures hover between 27°C and 33°C, with virtually no rainfall. Coastal resorts in Phu Quoc, Mui Ne, and Con Dao offer ideal beach conditions. Lunar New Year celebrations transform the streets with vibrant peach blossoms and traditional lanterns. Experiencing Tet: Lunar New Year in Vietnam Tet is the core of Vietnamese culture. While travelling during the actual 3-4 days of Tet requires careful planning (as transport is booked out and many shops close), it is a magical time to witness traditions. Streets are filled with yellow apricot blossoms, red lanterns, and families preparing traditional foods like banh chung (sticky rice cakes). mainEntity.name: Is January a good time to visit Halong Bay?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, but expect cooler, misty weather. While it is rarely rainy, morning fog is common, which actually adds a dramatic, mystical feel to the limestone karsts. You will need a jacket for the sundeck.

mainEntity.name: Is it warm enough to swim in Hoi An in January?

acceptedAnswer.text: It is borderline. Sea temperatures are around 22°C (71°F) and the breeze can be cool. While sunny days are perfect for swimming, overcast days might feel a bit chilly. For guaranteed swimming weather, head further south to Nha Trang or Phu Quoc.

mainEntity.name: Does Tet (Lunar New Year) happen in January?

acceptedAnswer.text: Tet typically falls between late January and mid-February. The week of Tet is a national holiday when many shops, restaurants, and museums close. However, the 2-3 weeks leading up to Tet are an incredible time to visit, as the cities are decorated and markets are bustling.

jsonLd.description: Vietnam's greatest adventures lie beyond the tourist circuit — the Ha Giang karst plateau, Phong Nha's cathedral caves, and the forests of Ba Be National Park. Private adventure tours for genuine explorers.

mainEntity.name: How do I book access to Son Doong Cave?

acceptedAnswer.text: Son Doong is open for only 4 months per year (February to August) and permits are limited to 1,000 visitors. The 4-day expedition costs approximately US$3,000-4,000 per person. We hold relationships with Oxalis Adventure Tours, the sole authorised operator, and can advise on current waiting list status and application process.

mainEntity.name: What fitness level is required for adventure tours in Vietnam?

acceptedAnswer.text: This varies dramatically by activity. Ha Giang by private 4x4 requires no particular fitness. Ha Giang by motorcycle requires riding experience and basic fitness. Phong Nha cave treks involve 10-15km of walking on rocky terrain — good fitness and no knee problems recommended. Son Doong is a 4-day jungle and cave expedition requiring excellent fitness and no fear of confined spaces.

mainEntity.name: Is there diving in Vietnam?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes — the Con Dao archipelago (off the south coast), Phu Quoc, and the waters around Nha Trang offer genuine diving experiences. Con Dao has the best visibility and coral health. March to September is the best dive season in the south. PADI certification courses are available at all major dive sites.

mainEntity.name: Can I combine adventure activities with cultural sightseeing?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, and we highly recommend it. Ha Giang combines naturally with Hanoi. Phong Nha can be reached from Hue or Da Nang as a 2-night extension. Ba Be National Park is 3 hours from Hanoi and makes an excellent pre- or post-tour addition. Con Dao is an independent island extension to a southern Vietnam itinerary.

mainEntity.name: What is Ba Be National Park?

acceptedAnswer.text: Ba Be is Vietnam's only natural freshwater lake, set within a 23,000-hectare national park of primary forest in the far north. The lake is surrounded by limestone mountains and home to an extraordinary diversity of bird and bat species. Accommodation is in village homestays beside the lake; activities include kayaking, jungle hiking, and visits to the Tay ethnic minority community who have lived here for centuries. It receives very few visitors and is one of the country's genuine hidden destinations.

pages.text: ADVENTURE Adventure Vietnam: Off the Beaten Track Tours Home > Inspirations > Adventure Tours 50 Vietnam Tours 14 Travel Guides 11 Places to visit 6 Hotels 6 Things to do 0 Vietnam Cruises 12 Best time to visit Vietnam's tourist circuit — Hanoi, Halong Bay, Hoi An, Ho Chi Minh City — is justifiably popular and genuinely extraordinary. But it represents perhaps 15% of a country that extends north to limestone peaks bordering China, west to jungle-covered mountains on the Laos border, and south to mangrove forests and offshore archipelagos that receive almost no visitor traffic. The off-the-beaten-track Vietnam — Ha Giang, Phong Nha, Ba Be National Park, the Central Highlands, the Con Dao islands — is a different country entirely: wilder, quieter, more demanding, and infinitely more rewarding for those who seek it. Ha Giang: Vietnam's Last Frontier Ha Giang Province in Vietnam's far north is the destination that has most dramatically emerged in the past five years. Its 350-kilometre loop through the Dong Van Karst Plateau — a UNESCO Global Geopark — crosses landscapes that have barely changed in centuries: H'Mong villages perched on cliff edges, markets where ethnic minorities from six different groups trade in the same square on Sunday mornings, roads that cling to cliff faces above gorges so deep that clouds sit at the bottom. The Ma Pi Leng Pass is the centrepiece: a 20-kilometre stretch of road carved into a limestone cliff face above the Nho Que River, 1,000 metres below. There is no comparative road experience in Southeast Asia. We offer the loop by private motorcycle (for experienced riders), by private 4x4 (for all fitness and experience levels), and by foot for those who want to trek between the H'Mong villages at human pace. The Ma Pi Leng Pass — 1,000 metres above the Nho Que River gorge, and the most dramatic road in Vietnam. Phong Nha: The World's Most Spectacular Caves Phong Nha-Ke Bang National Park in central Vietnam contains what were, until 2009, the world's largest known cave systems — and several that remain the largest. Son Doong Cave, discovered in 1991 and not entered by explorers until 2009, is so vast that it contains its own internal weather system: jungle, clouds, and a river that vanishes underground and resurfaces 30 kilometres away. Limited access to Son Doong (only 1,000 visitors per year, US$3,000 per person minimum) makes it the most exclusive adventure tourism experience in Asia. The queue for permits extends years in advance. We maintain waiting list access through our partnership with Oxalis Adventure Tours, the only operator authorised to run Son Doong expeditions. Paradise Cave, Tu Lan Cave, and Hang En (the world's third largest cave, with an underground river beach) are extraordinary alternatives with considerably easier access. Phong Nha's cave systems — some of the world's largest and most spectacular, now accessible via guided expeditions through certified operators. jsonLd.headline: Vietnam Culinary Inspiration: A Journey Through the Country's Food Soul
jsonLd.description: Get inspired for a Vietnam culinary journey — from Hanoi's dawn pho kitchens to Hoi An's ocean-to-table restaurants. Food travel inspiration from specialists who have eaten their way through Vietnam.

mainEntity.name: What is the best food city in Vietnam?

acceptedAnswer.text: Hoi An produces the most unique and distinctive cuisine — dishes that exist only in this town and nowhere else. Hanoi produces the most disciplined and perfectly executed food. Hue produces the most complex and ceremonially interesting cuisine. Saigon produces the greatest diversity. Every answer is defensible; every city deserves at least one full day of eating.

mainEntity.name: Is Vietnamese food generally spicy?

acceptedAnswer.text: Less spicy than most people expect. Northern Vietnamese food is not spicy at all. Central Vietnamese food can be quite hot (bun bo Hue especially). Southern Vietnamese food uses more chilli than the north but is still manageable for most Western palates. Spice is almost always added at the table, so you can control your own level.

mainEntity.name: Can I bring home Vietnamese ingredients?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes — fish sauce (Phu Quoc nuoc mam is the finest), dried rice noodles, pho spice packets, and Vietnamese coffee grounds all travel well and are freely available in good condition. Fresh herbs and produce cannot be brought back to the UK. Phu Quoc fish sauce, in particular, is one of the great food souvenirs.

mainEntity.name: Are Vietnamese cooking classes worth doing?

acceptedAnswer.text: Excellent ones are genuinely among the best travel experiences available in Vietnam. The key is choosing a class that starts at the market (not a pre-stocked kitchen), uses a private teacher (not a group demonstration), and produces dishes you will actually make at home. We book all cooking classes through vetted providers we have used personally.

mainEntity.name: What is Vietnamese coffee?

acceptedAnswer.text: Vietnamese coffee is made from dark-roasted robusta beans brewed through a small drip filter (phin) directly over sweetened condensed milk. It is strong, sweet, and completely unlike European espresso. Iced (ca phe da) or hot (ca phe nong), it is one of the great pleasures of travelling in Vietnam. The egg coffee (ca phe trung) of Hanoi — espresso topped with a meringue-like mixture of egg yolk and condensed milk — is extraordinary and must be tried.

pages.text: CULINARY Vietnam Culinary Inspiration: A Journey Through the Country's Food Soul Home > Inspirations > Culinary Inspiration 50 Vietnam Tours 14 Travel Guides 11 Places to visit 6 Hotels 6 Things to do 0 Vietnam Cruises 12 Best time to visit Vietnamese food is receiving its long-overdue recognition as one of the great culinary traditions of the world. Anthony Bourdain said it was the most complex and rewarding street food culture he encountered in 25 years of food travel. The Michelin Guide arrived in Vietnam in 2023 and found a food scene considerably more sophisticated than the international press had suggested. And yet the best Vietnamese food is still not in any restaurant — it is in the house behind the market stall, in the grandmother's kitchen, in the floating market boat where the cook has been making the same soup since 5am. This is the food we design culinary tours around. The Three Cuisines of Vietnam To understand Vietnamese food, you need to understand that the country's 1,650-kilometre length produces three genuinely distinct culinary traditions. Northern Vietnamese cooking (centred on Hanoi) is the most restrained: cleaner broths, fewer herbs, almost no sugar, a precision that rewards attention. Central Vietnamese cooking (Hue and Hoi An) is the most complex: layered, ceremonial, influenced by centuries of imperial court tradition and the particular geography of the central coast. Southern Vietnamese cooking (Ho Chi Minh City and the Mekong Delta) is the most abundant: sweeter, richer, more Chinese and Cambodian in influence, shaped by the extraordinary productivity of the Mekong Delta's rice bowl. A culinary tour connecting all three is not repetitive — each region's food reveals a completely different country. Hoi An's food culture is the most distinctive in Vietnam — its iconic dishes are specific to the town and cannot be authentically replicated elsewhere. The Dishes That Define Vietnam Pho: The north's defining contribution to world cuisine. A bowl of pho at its best — perfect broth, silky noodles, translucent beef — is one of the genuinely perfect foods. Find it at Pho Thin on Dinh Tien Hoang in Hanoi, open from 6am until it runs out (usually 10am). Bun cha: Grilled pork in a light fish-sauce broth with cold rice noodles and fresh herbs. The dish Barack Obama ate on his last trip to Vietnam. Find it at Bun Cha Huong Lien on Ly Van Phuc. Banh mi: The Vietnamese baguette sandwich, now recognised globally but still best in Vietnam — specifically at Banh Mi Phuong on Phan Chu Trinh in Hoi An, where the baguettes are baked fresh every two hours and the filling combinations are precise to the point of art. Cao lau: Hoi An's signature noodle dish, made only with water from the Ba Le ancient well and only in this town. If you eat it elsewhere, it is not the same dish. Bun bo Hue: The central city's great noodle soup, fiercer and more complex than pho, with lemongrass at its heart and a spice level that ranges from gentle to genuinely alarming. The best version is at a stall on Nguyen Chi Thanh that opens at 6am and sells out by 9. jsonLd.headline: Vietnam Family Tours: Extraordinary Adventures for All Ages
jsonLd.description: Vietnam is one of Asia's most rewarding family travel destinations. Private family tours with activities for all ages, child-friendly accommodation, and itineraries that keep both parents and children genuinely engaged.

mainEntity.name: What age is appropriate for a Vietnam family tour?

acceptedAnswer.text: Children from age 5 upwards manage the standard family itinerary very well. Children from age 8 can participate in kayaking, cycling, and cooking classes. Teenagers consistently rate Vietnam among their most memorable travel destinations — the food culture, the history, and the landscape all engage strongly with older children.

mainEntity.name: Are Vietnamese hotels suitable for families?

acceptedAnswer.text: The best hotels in Vietnam accommodate families very well. Family rooms (king bed plus twins) are standard at 4 and 5-star properties. Interconnecting rooms are available at most luxury hotels. Properties like the Park Hyatt Saigon, Four Seasons Nam Hai, and Silk Path Sapa all have excellent family facilities including pools, children's activity programmes, and family dining options.

mainEntity.name: Is the food safe for children?

acceptedAnswer.text: Vietnamese food is generally very clean and safe for children. Fresh ingredients, immediate preparation, and the absence of heavy sauces or extreme spicing at most restaurants makes it child-friendly. We recommend avoiding street stalls that cannot be verified for freshness; our guides always steer families to reliable establishments. Bottled water should always be used.

mainEntity.name: How do we handle food allergies on a Vietnam family tour?

acceptedAnswer.text: We communicate all dietary requirements and allergies to every restaurant, hotel, and cooking class host in writing and in Vietnamese before arrival. Vietnam has excellent options for most common allergies. Severe nut allergies require careful management — we advise on this specifically during the planning process.

mainEntity.name: Can grandparents come on a family tour of Vietnam?

acceptedAnswer.text: Absolutely. Our multigenerational family tours account for a wide range of mobility and energy levels. All activities are optional; private vehicles ensure grandparents can rest whenever needed. The hotel selections all have pool access and comfortable common areas. Many grandparents report Vietnam as among the most engaging and manageable international trips they have taken.

pages.text: FAMILY Vietnam Family Tours: Extraordinary Adventures for All Ages Home > Inspirations > Family Tours 50 Vietnam Tours 14 Travel Guides 11 Places to visit 6 Hotels 6 Things to do 0 Vietnam Cruises 12 Best time to visit Travelling Vietnam with children is one of the most rewarding things a family can do together. The country is extraordinarily welcoming to children — Vietnamese culture places enormous value on family, and travelling with children opens doors to interactions that solo travellers never experience. The food culture is actively engaging for children of all ages; the landscape provides constant visual stimulation; the history is accessible and vivid without being overwhelming. A well-designed private family tour accounts for all ages, pacing that works for everyone, and experiences that parents and children genuinely share rather than parents dutifully enduring. What Makes Vietnam Ideal for Families Vietnamese people love children with a warmth that feels completely genuine. A family walking through Hanoi's Old Quarter or Hoi An's Ancient Town will be stopped constantly — by shopkeepers wanting to practise English, by elderly men who want to shake the children's hands, by market women who will press fruit into small palms as gifts. This social warmth is one of Vietnam's great gifts to family travellers, and no amount of guidebook reading can prepare you for how immediately it makes children feel welcome and interesting. The food is another natural engagement point. Children who are adventurous about food will find Vietnam overwhelming in the best possible way. Cooking classes designed for families — market in the morning, cooking at noon, eating what you made in the afternoon — are among the best experiences we offer for mixed-age groups. Even children who are initially cautious about unfamiliar food tend to open up after 48 hours in Vietnam's company. Kayaking through Halong Bay's limestone lagoons — one of the great family adventure experiences in Southeast Asia. The Best Family Experiences by Destination Hanoi: The Vietnam Museum of Ethnology has an excellent outdoor section with full-scale reconstructed houses from 54 ethnic groups — child-friendly and genuinely fascinating. Hoan Kiem Lake at 6am with locals doing tai chi and feeding terrapins. The Thang Long Water Puppet Theatre — one hour of extraordinary performance that works for ages 5 to 95. Halong Bay: Kayaking through hidden lagoons (most children aged 7+ can manage this with basic instruction). Swimming off the junk deck. Squid fishing from the bow deck at night with glow sticks. The cave visits are engaging for older children; the limestone formations look exactly like dragon scales, which the legend says they are. Hoi An: Bicycle riding through the paddy fields (flat, simple, child-friendly). Lantern making from a local craftsperson. The beach at An Bang is calm and safe for all ages. The cooking class at Red Bridge involves a river boat journey to reach the school, which is itself an adventure. Mekong Delta: Cycling on levee roads between paddy fields. Boat trips through the coconut candy workshops. The floating market at Cai Rang at dawn — a functioning wholesale market that operates like nothing children will ever have seen before. jsonLd.description: Discover why Vietnam has become one of Asia's premier golf destinations — championship courses against limestone karsts, coastal links, and mountain fairways at prices that surprise every visitor.

mainEntity.name: Which is Vietnam's best golf course?

acceptedAnswer.text: BRG Kings Island Mountain Course near Hanoi is consistently ranked first in Vietnam and among the best 10 in Southeast Asia. The Montgomerie Links in Da Nang is the most popular with visiting golfers who want a genuine coastal links experience. Ba Na Hills is the most visually spectacular. The correct answer depends on what type of course you prefer.

mainEntity.name: Can I play golf and see Vietnam's cultural highlights in the same trip?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes — this is precisely how we design our golf tours. Play Kings Island on the afternoon after arriving in Hanoi; spend the following day sightseeing in the Old Quarter. Halong Bay cruise before flying south to Da Nang; Montgomerie Links and Ba Na Hills over two days; Hoi An Ancient Town on the rest day; Laguna Lang Co on the way to Hue.

mainEntity.name: What is the dress code at Vietnamese golf courses?

acceptedAnswer.text: Smart casual is the standard at all major courses: collared shirt, tailored shorts or trousers. Denim is generally not permitted on the course. All courses have pro shops with clothing available if required. Dress codes are enforced at the clubhouse but are generally more relaxed on the course itself.

mainEntity.name: Are caddies available in Vietnam?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, and they are excellent. Caddies are mandatory at most major Vietnamese courses and cost between £15-25 for 18 holes (tip additional). Vietnamese caddies are well-trained, knowledgeable about their courses, and provide accurate yardage and reading advice. Using a caddy is highly recommended even for experienced golfers.

mainEntity.name: Can we arrange a golf tournament for a corporate group?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. We organise private corporate golf events at major Vietnamese courses for groups of 8-40 players, including tournament organisation, scoring, prizes, and post-round dining. All logistical elements — accommodation, transfers, tee time blocks — are arranged as part of a single programme.

pages.text: GOLF Vietnam Golf Inspiration: Asia's Most Beautiful Courses Home > Inspirations > Golf Inspiration 50 Vietnam Tours 14 Travel Guides 11 Places to visit 6 Hotels 6 Things to do 0 Vietnam Cruises 12 Best time to visit Ten years ago, Vietnam barely registered as a golf destination. Today, it hosts courses designed by Colin Montgomerie, Luke Donald, Sir Nick Faldo, and Lee Schmidt — championship designers who have delivered some of the most visually spectacular layouts in the world. The green fees are still a fraction of equivalent courses in Japan, South Korea, or the UK. The facilities have reached international standard. And the settings — limestone karst mountains, UNESCO lagoons, tropical coastlines — are completely without equivalent in the golfing world. Why Vietnam for Golf? There are three reasons golfers choose Vietnam over Thailand, Malaysia, or other Asian alternatives. First, the quality of the top courses is now genuinely world-class — not world-class-for-Asia but world-class by any standard. BRG Kings Island's Mountain Course, The Montgomerie Links, and Laguna Golf Lang Co would all rank comfortably among the finest courses in Europe if they were located there. Second, the settings are incomparable. No golf destination in the world offers fairways overlooking active UNESCO World Heritage Sites, with limestone karst formations providing the backdrop for approach shots. Third, the cost. Green fees at Vietnam's finest courses run from £40 to £120 for 18 holes — less than half the equivalent at comparable courses in most European markets. BRG Kings Island Mountain Course at dawn — where the karst landscape provides the most dramatic natural backdrop of any golf course in Southeast Asia. Course by Course: The Essential Vietnam Golf List BRG Kings Island Golf Resort (Hanoi): 45 holes across three courses, the Mountain Course being the standout. Designed by Lee Schmidt, it uses the karst landscape of Dong Mo Lake to extraordinary visual effect. Consistently ranked Vietnam's best course and among the top ten in Southeast Asia. The Montgomerie Links (Da Nang): Colin Montgomerie's signature course runs along 5 kilometres of pristine Vietnamese coastline. A genuine links experience in a tropical climate, with the South China Sea visible from most holes. Green fees from approximately £80. Ba Na Hills Golf Club (Da Nang): Luke Donald's 2016 masterwork, built at altitude in the forest above Da Nang. Views of the central Vietnamese coast from the higher holes; forest and ravine holes in the valleys below. The most visually dramatic course in central Vietnam. Laguna Golf Lang Co (Hue/Da Nang): Sir Nick Faldo's signature course on a spit of land between the Lang Co lagoon and the South China Sea. One of the most naturally beautiful settings of any course in Southeast Asia. Attached to the Angsana Lang Co resort. mainEntity.name: What is the most exclusive experience available in Vietnam?

acceptedAnswer.text: Cave dining in Halong Bay — a single private table set inside a volcanic sea cave, accessible only by kayak from your chartered junk, with a private chef and full wine service — is the experience we most consistently hear described as life-changing. mainEntity.name: How much does a luxury Vietnam tour cost?

acceptedAnswer.text: A fully private luxury tour — private guide, private vehicle, 5-star accommodation, two-night private junk charter, domestic flights — typically costs from £280-400 per person per day for a couple. Ultra-luxury experiences (Amanoi, Six Senses, private helicopter) move this higher. We will give you a precise quote based on your specific requirements.

mainEntity.name: Can we have a completely private Halong Bay cruise?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. The Heritage Line, Indochine Sail, and a handful of other premium operators offer full private charter of their vessels. A typical private charter for 8 cabins (accommodating 2-16 guests depending on sharing) costs approximately £3,000-8,000 per night depending on the vessel. This includes all food, beverages, kayaks, excursions, and crew.

mainEntity.name: What luxury accommodation is available in Hanoi?

The La Siesta Premium is an excellent boutique alternative with outstanding service. For something more contemporary, the Capella Hanoi opened in 2021 in a beautifully converted French colonial building.

pages.text: LUXURY Vietnam Luxury Tours: The Ultimate Private Travel Experience Home > Inspirations > Luxury Tours 50 Vietnam Tours 14 Travel Guides 11 Places to visit 6 Hotels 6 Things to do 0 Vietnam Cruises 12 Best time to visit The word "luxury" has been so thoroughly devalued in travel marketing that it no longer carries reliable meaning. A five-star hotel in Vietnam can mean anything from a genuinely exceptional resort to a large, impersonal city block with a rooftop pool. What we mean by luxury is more specific: a private junk with 8 cabins for your group of four. A private guide who knows which museum director to call for after-hours access to the Hue Citadel. A single table in a cave in Halong Bay, set for two, with a private chef and a view of the karsts at midnight. Luxury in Vietnam is experiential before it is material — and the experiences available here have no equivalent anywhere else. The Finest Accommodation in Vietnam The Amanoi at Ninh Van Bay, accessible only by speedboat from Nha Trang, remains the most extraordinary resort in the country: 35 pavilions and villas built into a granite hillside above a UNESCO-protected national park bay. The Amandari principle — no lobbies, no signage, complete privacy — is executed in Vietnam with particular elegance. The pools are carved into the rock. The dining pavilion hangs over the bay. The spa is set among boulders in a private cove. The Four Seasons Nam Hai near Hoi An represents a different kind of luxury: 100 pool villas on Ha My Beach, three pool complexes descending to the sea, an extraordinary spa, and a culinary programme that draws from the Hoi An food culture surrounding it. The Heritage Line's Jasmine and Au Co — the finest junk boats on Halong Bay — represent luxury afloat: teakwood cabins, private sun decks, wines chosen by a sommelier, a route that avoids the crowded central bay for the quieter Lan Ha waters. Private villa dining with bay views — the defining image of Vietnam's ultra-luxury resort experience. Exclusive Access and Private Experiences The experiences that define genuine luxury travel are those unavailable to the general visitor. A private dawn visit to the Hue Citadel before the doors open to the public — arranged through our relationship with the Hue Monuments Conservation Centre. A cooking lesson in the home of a family who has been cooking imperial Vietnamese cuisine for three generations and has never appeared in a guidebook. A private boat to a section of Halong Bay that no cruise operator serves regularly, with snorkelling in water so clear the coral is visible from the surface. Cave dining in Halong Bay — a single table set inside a volcanic rock cave, accessible only by kayak, with a private chef who has prepared the menu aboard your junk — is available only through a handful of operators who maintain relationships with the national park authority. We are among them. Phi ceremony at a private home in Hue, a private calligraphy lesson with a master practitioner in Hanoi's Old Quarter, a dawn sesame-oil pressing demonstration in a 200-year-old merchant house in Hoi An — these are the experiences that no online booking platform can arrange. They require relationships built over years. Private Charters: Air, Sea, and Road At the highest tier of luxury travel in Vietnam, the vehicle is itself part of the experience. A private helicopter transfer from Da Nang to Hue (12 minutes, following the coastline over the Hai Van Pass) replaces a 2-hour road journey with one of the great aerial views in Southeast Asia. A private junk with eight cabins occupied entirely by your group of six — no other guests, your schedule, your route, your menu — on Halong Bay transforms the most popular attraction in Vietnam into something genuinely private. On the road, the finest private vehicle available in Vietnam is the Toyota Land Cruiser V8 with a dedicated driver: air-conditioned, supremely comfortable, and large enough for four passengers with significant luggage. For groups, private minibuses maintain the same standard of cleanliness, driver training, and flexibility. Private domestic flights can be chartered for groups of 6-12 on select routes. In Hanoi, the capital, take in delicious meals in lovely French colonial villas, shop at chic boutiques, and explore the charming Old Quarter. Travel south to Hoi An, a UNESCO site, where you can visit beautifully preserved merchant homes, wander through lively markets, and lounge on lovely beaches. In Saigon (Ho Chi Minh City), you can tour vibrant markets, explore art galleries, or have a local tailor make a custom ao dai for you to wear. There are also so many natural wonders outside the cities. You can sail through stunning limestone formations in Halong Bay, hike to hill tribe villages and rice paddies near Sapa, or kayak along the relaxed waters of the Mekong Delta. pages.text: Overview Capture the essence of Vietnam with this sweeping trip from the charming northern capital, Hanoi, to metropolitan Ho Chi Minh City in the south. Cruise for two days through spectacular Ha Long Bay, with floating karst peaks scattered for miles across emerald waters. Admire the country’s most beautiful ancient architecture in Hoi An, ride a bamboo basket boat in Cam Thanh Village, and explore the immense network of underground tunnels at Cu Chi. Beyond the country’s major highlights, delve deeper into the everyday lives of Vietnamese with this eleven-day trip. headings: Born from a love of Vietnam, built for those who seek more than a holiday.
pages.text: Est. 2008 Our Story A decade and a half of crafting extraordinary journeys through Indochina's heart. Where It Began Born from a love of Vietnam, built for those who seek more than a holiday. Vietnam Heritage Tours was founded in 2008 by a small team of passionate travellers who had fallen irreversibly in love with Vietnam. They had witnessed the country's transformation — its ancient temples standing firm beside gleaming new cities, its fishing villages humming with the same rhythms as they had for centuries — and they wanted to share that wonder with the world. What began as a handful of carefully curated itineraries for friends and colleagues has grown into one of the most trusted names in luxury Vietnam travel. Yet our founding principle has never changed: every journey we design must be as extraordinary as the country it explores. Our Values What We Believe In Authenticity Above All We reject the superficial. Every experience we recommend — every guide, every lodge, every meal — has been personally vetted by our specialists. If it doesn't feel real, it doesn't make the cut. Responsible Luxury We believe that privilege comes with responsibility. Our journeys support local communities, champion sustainable practices, and leave destinations better than we found them. Bespoke by Nature We do not sell packages — we create experiences. Every itinerary begins with a conversation, and ends with a journey that is entirely, unmistakably yours. A Journey of Our Own Milestones 2008 Founded in Hanoi with a team of five specialists and a shared love of authentic Vietnamese travel. 2011 Expanded to cover Cambodia and Laos, offering full Indochina journey planning. 2015 Recognised by Condé Nast Traveller as one of Southeast Asia's leading boutique operators. 2019 Launched our Responsible Travel Charter, committing to carbon-conscious, community-first itineraries. 2024 Proud to have guided over 12,000 travellers and counting — each journey as personal as the last. jsonLd.headline: The Mekong Delta by Sampan: Vietnam's Other World
jsonLd.description: The Mekong Delta is a world of water — 22,000km of canals, floating markets, stilted homes, and river life unchanged for centuries. A sampan journey through its back-channels is unlike anything else in Vietnam.

mainEntity.name: Is the Mekong Delta worth visiting if I only have one day?

acceptedAnswer.text: A day trip from Ho Chi Minh City gives you a taste, but the back-canal experience — which is the genuine article — requires two days minimum. If you have only one day, hire a private boat rather than joining a group tour and instruct your guide to take you away from the standard tourist circuit.

mainEntity.name: What's the best way to get from Ho Chi Minh City to the Delta?

acceptedAnswer.text: Private car to Can Tho (3.5 hours on the expressway) is the most comfortable option. The Cao Lanh Bridge opened in 2018 significantly improved the journey. A hydrofoil boat from the Bach Dang pier in Saigon to My Tho takes 75 minutes and is a good option if you want to arrive by water.

mainEntity.name: Are the floating markets tourist attractions or real markets?

acceptedAnswer.text: Cai Rang is a functioning wholesale market — the traders are buying and selling real quantities of produce for the restaurant and food industry supply chain. However, because of the early timing, the majority of visitors are tourists rather than wholesale buyers by the time the day-trippers arrive (after 8am). Go before 6:30am if you want to see it as a working market.

pages.text: Home › Things To Do › Mekong Delta Boat Journey RIVER JOURNEYS The Mekong Delta by Sampan: Vietnam's Other World Twenty-two thousand kilometres of canals. A world where the road is always water. 🕒 7 min read | 📍 Can Tho | ⭐ Easy. Comfortable seated sampan journeys on flat water. 50 Vietnam Tours 14 Travel Guides 11 Places to visit 6 Hotels 6 Things to do 0 Vietnam Cruises 12 Best time to visit If Ho Chi Minh City is the engine of modern Vietnam, the Mekong Delta is the country's heartbeat. The nine tributaries of the Mekong River fan out across the southernmost tip of Vietnam into an interlocking system of waterways so dense that from the air it looks like the veins of a leaf. Twenty-two thousand kilometres of canals connect 17 million people who live almost entirely by and on the water. Floating markets sell fruit piled in wooden boats. Houses on stilts line channels barely wide enough for a sampan. Children use boats the way city children use bicycles — to get to school, to the market, to each other's houses. Coming here from the cities of central or northern Vietnam is like arriving in a different country, operating according to entirely different laws. What Makes This Experience Special ✦ Float through Cai Rang Floating Market — the largest in the Mekong Delta, largest before 8am ✦ Navigate the narrow back-canals of Ben Tre province by traditional wooden sampan ✦ Visit a coconut candy workshop, a rice paper factory, and a honey bee farm on the same morning ✦ Cross the Mekong by local ferry — the way 17 million Delta residents travel every day ✦ Cycle through Vinh Long's fruit orchards and try 30 varieties of tropical fruit with a local family ✦ Stay overnight on a river homestay and eat dinner with the fishing family whose boat is also their home Cai Rang Floating Market: Early Morning or Nothing The floating market at Cai Rang, six kilometres south of Can Tho on the Hau River, is the largest wholesale floating market in the Mekong Delta. Hundreds of wooden boats cluster together before dawn, each one loaded with a single product — watermelons stacked five deep, pineapples in nets, dragonfruit in towers — and a bẹo (a long pole with a sample of the cargo hanging from the end so buyers can identify the product from a distance). The market peaks between 5:30am and 7:30am. By 9am it's largely done. Every travel guide tells you to go early. Almost no one actually does it — because getting from Can Tho to the market at 5:30am requires getting up at 4:45am, which tests even the most committed traveller. I did it twice. The first visit, I arrived at 7am and thought it was excellent. The second, at 5:30am, I understood it. In the pre-dawn dark with the market boats lit only by their own lanterns, everything moving on the water, the sound of the vendors calling and the boat engines and the river birds, the atmosphere is of something primeval and irreplaceable. UNESCO's representative body recommended Cai Rang for inclusion on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2016. The back-canals of Ben Tre province. Roads here are an afterthought; the canals are the infrastructure. Ben Tre Province: The Back-Canals That Most Visitors Miss The standard Mekong day trip from Ho Chi Minh City goes to My Tho, sees one floating market, visits a honey farm and a coconut candy workshop on the same island, and turns around. The experience is not wrong, but it's the Mekong's lobby. The rooms beyond — the labyrinthine back-canal system of Ben Tre province — are where the actual substance lives. Ben Tre is known as the "Land of the Coconut Palm." The province produces 40% of Vietnam's coconut output and the trees are everywhere — lining every canal bank, shading every house, providing the raw material for an industry that makes candy, oil, rope, cooking utensils, and roofing material. Navigating Ben Tre's back-canals by sampan with a local guide takes you through passages where the canopy meets overhead, the water turns dark green with reflected light, and you travel for twenty minutes without seeing any sign of the 21st century except the occasional solar panel on a house roof. At the end of one canal is Nguyen Thi Thanh's home — a stilted house where she has been making rice paper by hand for forty years. She spreads the batter across a curved bamboo mat, steams it for ninety seconds over a clay pot, peels it off, and sets it on a bamboo rack to dry in the sun. The result is translucent, slightly chewy rice paper that bears no resemblance to the dried variety sold in Western supermarkets. Homestay on the Water: Staying With a River Family The Mekong Delta has excellent homestay accommodation — families who take guests into their river houses, feed them from their own garden and fishing catch, and treat the experience as genuine hospitality rather than a commercial transaction. The best are in Vinh Long province, where the homestay culture has been developing since the late 1990s and the families have learned to provide comfortable accommodation without losing the authenticity that makes the experience meaningful. At Ut Trinh's homestay on An Binh Island, you sleep in a room above the river on a wooden platform that sways slightly with the current. Dinner is whatever was caught or harvested that day — catfish from the river, morning glory from the garden, green papaya salad, rice from the family's own paddies. After dinner, Ut's husband Mr. Thanh sits on the platform with a bottle of rice wine and tells stories — about the American War, about the floods of 2000 when the water rose two metres above this platform, about his daughter who now lives in Ho Chi Minh City and works in a phone repair shop. The gap between his world and hers, across sixty kilometres of Delta water, is one of the most quietly startling things I encountered in Vietnam. Duration 2 days minimum to do it justice. 3 days ideal with overnight homestay. Difficulty Easy. Comfortable seated sampan journeys on flat water. mainEntity.name: When exactly does the Lantern Festival happen?

acceptedAnswer.text: The 14th day of every lunar month — roughly once per calendar month but falling on different dates each time. In 2025, notable dates include 11 February, 13 March, 12 April, 12 May. Your guide can confirm the exact date for your travel period.

mainEntity.name: Is the festival worth visiting outside the full moon date?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes — Hoi An is permanently beautiful after dark, and the lanterns are always lit in the Ancient Town. But the full-moon night has a specific quality that the other nights don't — the streets are closed to motorbikes, the electric lights are dimmed, and the community participates collectively in a way that feels like something more than tourism.

mainEntity.name: Where should I stay to be closest to the festival?

acceptedAnswer.text: Any property within or adjacent to the Ancient Town. The Anantara Hoi An Resort on the riverside is excellent — you can watch lanterns float past from your room. Almanity and La Maison 1888 at InterContinental Danang Sun Peninsula are also within easy reach by car.

pages.text: Home › Things To Do › Hoi An Lantern Festival FESTIVALS & CULTURE Hoi An's Full Moon Lantern Festival: The Most Beautiful Night in Vietnam At 8pm on the 14th lunar day, the electricity switches off and 400 years of history reappear under silk lanterns. 🕒 6 min read | 📍 Hoi An Ancient Town | ⭐ Easy walking on flat ancient town streets 50 Vietnam Tours 14 Travel Guides 11 Places to visit 6 Hotels 6 Things to do 0 Vietnam Cruises 12 Best time to visit On the 14th day of every lunar month, Hoi An Ancient Town undergoes a transformation that has been repeating for four centuries. The electric lights go off. The streets fill with the glow of hundreds of silk lanterns hung from every building, floating in baskets on the Thu Bon River, carried by visitors and locals alike. The sound changes too — the motorbikes disappear, the music becomes traditional, and the narrow lanes of the Ancient Town fill with something that feels genuinely ancient, not reconstructed. I have been to many things billed as "the most magical night in Vietnam." This is the one that actually delivers. What Makes This Experience Special ✦ Every 14th day of the lunar month — typically once per calendar month ✦ Release a floating flower lantern (đèn hoa đăng) on the Thu Bon River for luck ✦ Walk the lamplit streets of the UNESCO World Heritage Ancient Town after dark ✦ Visit the Japanese Covered Bridge — built in 1593 — under lantern glow ✦ Watch traditional music and dance performed on the riverside stage ✦ Browse the night market stalls selling hand-made silk lanterns from local artisans What Actually Happens on Lantern Night The festival begins at dusk, when the Ancient Town switches off its commercial lighting and the street lamps are dimmed. The transition takes about ten minutes — you're in a busy tourist town, and then, almost imperceptibly, you're somewhere else. The lanterns that every building hangs year-round finally do the job they're designed for: without electric competition, their glow is soft, warm, and sufficient to walk by. The market stalls set up along Nguyen Huu Huan Street sell hand-made silk lanterns, flower crowns, and the small floating lanterns — rice paper over a bamboo frame, with a birthday-cake candle inside — that you carry down to the river and release. The river release is the emotional centre of the festival. You kneel at the bank, light the candle, say whatever you came here to say, and let the current take it. On a full festival night there can be five hundred lanterns drifting downstream simultaneously, each one a small orange star on the dark water. The Thu Bon River south of the Ancient Town is wide and slow, and the lanterns travel a long way before the candle finally burns out. The Full Moon Festival on the riverfront. Every building in the Ancient Town hangs lanterns year-round; on festival night, they become the only light source. The History Behind the Light Hoi An was Vietnam's most important trading port from the 15th to 19th centuries, a meeting point for Chinese, Japanese, Dutch, Portuguese, and Indian merchants. The Japanese community was so significant that an entire quarter of the town was designated for Japanese residences — the Covered Bridge at the western end of the old town was built by Japanese merchants in 1593 to connect their quarter to the Chinese quarter across the canal. The lantern tradition is a synthesis of all these cultures: Japanese obon festival lighting, Chinese lunar calendar observance, and Vietnamese custom combined into something that belongs entirely to Hoi An. The Ancient Town was designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1999. Its extraordinary preservation — 1,107 monuments including merchant houses, assembly halls, temples, and the bridge — is partly explained by its economic decline in the 19th century when the Thu Bon River silted up and sea trade moved north to Da Nang. The town that modernity forgot became the town history preserved. How to Do the Festival Without the Crowd The festival attracts large numbers, and the central streets can become very congested between 8pm and 10pm. The intelligent approach is to arrive early — be in the Ancient Town by 5:30pm, find a riverside table at a café on Bach Dang Street, and watch the transition from day to festival-night from a fixed position with a drink in hand. The peak crowd density is on Tran Phu and Le Loi streets. The parallel streets one block south — Nguyen Thai Hoc and Bach Dang along the river — are quieter and, many would argue, more beautiful. For the river lantern release, go to the riverbank on Le Loi Street rather than the more crowded Hoi An Riverside. The view downstream from there, with the Japanese Bridge visible in the distance and the lanterns floating between you, is the photograph that every travel magazine wants. It's also genuinely moving, regardless of how many times you've seen photographs of it.
